topic: Why Kinmen, Taiwan, is stranger than you think
hook: Your beach on Kinmen, Taiwan, faces a Chinese skyline, and the island's kitchen knives were once bombs.
title: Why Kinmen Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
Kinmen belongs to Taiwan, yet it sits only a few kilometres from the Chinese city of Xiamen. In this video you will see six true facts about the island: the skyline across the water, phones that can join a Chinese network, tap water that comes through a pipe from China, life under military rule until 1992, a war fought with loudspeakers, and kitchen knives made from bombs.

#Kinmen #Taiwan #StrangePlaces
tags: Why Kinmen is stranger than you think
comment_prompt: Which Kinmen fact surprised you most?

scenes.narration: Your beach on Kinmen, Taiwan, faces a Chinese skyline, and the island's kitchen knives were once bombs.
scenes.headline: Taiwan Faces China

scenes.narration: Kinmen belongs to Taiwan, yet it sits only a few kilometres from the Chinese city of Xiamen, across a narrow strip of water.
scenes.headline: A Few Kilometres Away

scenes.narration: Taiwan's main island is far away across the sea, but this small island is almost touching the coast of China.
scenes.headline: Far From Taiwan

scenes.narration: By the end you will see how a bomb became a knife, and why that is only part of the story.
scenes.headline: A Bomb Became A Knife

scenes.narration: Six strange facts are coming, and each one is stranger than the one before it.
scenes.headline: Six Strange Facts

scenes.narration: Stay for the last one, because it explains how this island ended up this way.
scenes.headline: Stay For The Last One

scenes.narration: Fact one: you can stand on Taiwanese land and look straight at the buildings of another country.
scenes.headline: Fact One: The Skyline

scenes.narration: Take a boat to Kinmen, walk to the shore that faces Xiamen, and just look across the water.
scenes.headline: Take The Boat

scenes.narration: You can see a modern skyline with tall towers and cranes, and every one of those buildings is in mainland China.
scenes.headline: Towers In China

scenes.narration: Xiamen is a large port city in Fujian province, with millions of people living in full view of this small island.
scenes.headline: Xiamen Is Huge

scenes.narration: Imagine standing in your own city and seeing a rival country's towers just across a narrow strip of sea.
scenes.headline: A Rival Across The Sea

scenes.narration: And Kinmen is nowhere near the rest of Taiwan. It sits much closer to China than it does to Taipei.
scenes.headline: Closer To China

scenes.narration: Older maps spell the name Quemoy, and during the Cold War this small island was a famous flashpoint.
scenes.headline: Also Called Quemoy

scenes.narration: Even the clock matches China. Kinmen, Xiamen and Taipei all share one time, which is two and a half hours ahead of India.
scenes.headline: Same Clock As China

scenes.narration: People on both sides of the water also grew up speaking the same Hokkien dialect, also called Minnan.
scenes.headline: Same Dialect

scenes.narration: So the voices sound alike, but the flags are different. Now, fact two, which happens right inside your pocket.
scenes.headline: Different Flags

scenes.narration: Fact two: on Kinmen, your phone can get confused about which country it is standing in.
scenes.headline: Fact Two: Your Phone

scenes.narration: Phones look for the strongest signal, and on the Xiamen side of the water there are Chinese mobile towers very close by.
scenes.headline: Towers Across The Water

scenes.narration: Visitors and locals have reported their phones joining a Chinese network and sending a welcome message from China.
scenes.headline: Welcome To China

scenes.narration: A roaming warning can pop up even though you never left Taiwan, and you never boarded a ship or a plane.
scenes.headline: Roaming Warning

scenes.narration: Signals do not care about borders, and on Kinmen the border is only water, which radio waves cross very easily.
scenes.headline: Signals Ignore Borders

scenes.narration: Now think about what a place this close to China had to prepare for in the past.
scenes.headline: Ready For Attack

scenes.narration: In 1949, soldiers from the Chinese mainland tried to land on Kinmen near a village called Guningtou.
scenes.headline: The 1949 Landing

scenes.narration: The defenders won that battle, and it is the main reason Kinmen is still under Taiwan today.
scenes.headline: Why Kinmen Stayed

scenes.narration: Some beaches still have rows of steel spikes stuck in the sand, built to rip open landing boats.
scenes.headline: Spikes In The Sand

scenes.narration: Guningtou is still remembered on the island with a museum and a memorial.
scenes.headline: A Museum Of War

scenes.narration: Those spikes are still there for tourists to photograph. But fact three is about something you drink every day.
scenes.headline: Next: Your Water

scenes.narration: Fact three: some of the water running out of Kinmen's taps travels from China.
scenes.headline: Fact Three: Tap Water

scenes.narration: Kinmen is small and often short of fresh water, so for years the island has had to think hard about every drop.
scenes.headline: A Thirsty Island

scenes.narration: In 2018, a pipeline opened that carries water under the sea from the Chinese side, in Fujian province, to Kinmen.
scenes.headline: A Pipe Under The Sea

scenes.narration: The water comes from the Chinese side because that is the nearest big supply, a short distance from where Kinmen sits.
scenes.headline: The Nearest Supply

scenes.narration: Think about that: two governments that are political rivals, connected by one pipe that runs under the sea.
scenes.headline: Rivals Share A Pipe

scenes.narration: There was already a ferry link before that. Since 2001, boats have run between Kinmen and the city of Xiamen.
scenes.headline: Ferry Since 2001

scenes.narration: For years, people used that ferry for family visits, shopping and trade, on the same water that once carried warships.
scenes.headline: Families And Trade

scenes.narration: Before the ferry, that stretch of sea was a front line with guns pointing across it in both directions.
scenes.headline: Once A Front Line

scenes.narration: Soon you will hear how bad that front line got. But first, fact four, about who ran the island.
scenes.headline: Who Ran The Island?

scenes.narration: Fact four: until 1992, ordinary families on Kinmen lived under military rule.
scenes.headline: Fact Four: Army Rule

scenes.narration: The army, not a normal local government, ran daily life on the island for decades, with curfews and travel limits.
scenes.headline: Curfews And Limits

scenes.narration: Soldiers were stationed all over this small island, and the whole place was built to survive an attack from the sea.
scenes.headline: Built For War

scenes.narration: They dug tunnels by hand through solid rock, including the Zhaishan tunnel, which was cut so boats could hide inside a hill.
scenes.headline: Tunnels Dug By Hand

scenes.narration: Boats could shelter and unload inside the hill, safe from enemy fire, and tourists can walk through part of it today.
scenes.headline: A Harbour Inside A Hill

scenes.narration: Villages on Kinmen also have stone wind lions, guardian statues set on roofs and at village edges.
scenes.headline: Wind Lion Guardians

scenes.narration: People believed the wind lions calmed the strong winds on the island, so even the statues have a job here.
scenes.headline: Statues With A Job

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places and facts like these, subscribe, because there are plenty more places that sound fake but are real.
scenes.headline: More Strange Places

scenes.narration: Back to Kinmen. The soldiers had good reason to be nervous, and fact five shows how tense it got.
scenes.headline: Tension Rises

scenes.narration: Fact five: for years, the two sides fought each other with giant loudspeakers and music.
scenes.headline: Fact Five: Loudspeakers

scenes.narration: On Kinmen, huge speakers pointed across the water at China, and speakers on the other side pointed right back.
scenes.headline: Speakers Face Speakers

scenes.narration: Taiwan's side played songs, including music by the famous singer Teresa Teng, whose songs were frowned on in mainland China.
scenes.headline: Teresa Teng's Songs

scenes.narration: The speakers also carried news and messages meant to change minds, not just to make noise.
scenes.headline: Messages To Change Minds

scenes.narration: At Beishan there is a long concrete wall full of speaker openings that was built to face the mainland.
scenes.headline: The Broadcasting Wall

scenes.narration: Imagine trying to sleep with a speaker war going on across a narrow strip of sea.
scenes.headline: Try Sleeping Here

scenes.narration: At Mashan, there is an observation post where visitors can look at the Chinese coast through binoculars.
scenes.headline: Binoculars At Mashan

scenes.narration: Past the water, the Chinese island of Dadeng is easy to spot from there.
scenes.headline: Dadeng Island, China

scenes.narration: Today, some of those speakers are tourist sights, and you can walk right up to them.
scenes.headline: War Gear As Sights

scenes.narration: Eventually the speakers fell silent. But the loudspeakers were the gentle part of this fight.
scenes.headline: The Speakers Fall Silent

scenes.narration: The last fact is the biggest one, and it is the reason for the knives in the hook.
scenes.headline: The Biggest Fact

scenes.narration: Fact six: in 1958, China began firing heavy artillery at Kinmen, shell after shell.
scenes.headline: Fact Six: 1958

scenes.narration: It is known as the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis, and Kinmen was right at the centre of it.
scenes.headline: Second Strait Crisis

scenes.narration: Underground shelters and tunnels became part of daily life, because the sky above the island was not safe.
scenes.headline: Life Underground

scenes.narration: The shelling later settled into a strange pattern: China fired on odd-numbered days only.
scenes.headline: Odd Days Only

scenes.narration: Even days were quiet, so islanders learned to plan their lives by the calendar.
scenes.headline: Life By The Calendar

scenes.narration: Some of the shells were not even explosive. They were filled with propaganda leaflets instead.
scenes.headline: Shells Full Of Leaflets

scenes.narration: That odd-day shelling went on for more than twenty years, and it finally stopped in 1979.
scenes.headline: Stopped In 1979

scenes.narration: Soldiers on both sides spent years watching each other, each side knowing the other was only a short boat ride away.
scenes.headline: Watching Each Other

scenes.narration: Islanders were left with a huge amount of metal: shell casings and bomb pieces lying all over the place.
scenes.headline: Metal Everywhere

scenes.narration: A local man named Wu Tseng-tung had an idea: melt that metal and turn it into kitchen knives.
scenes.headline: Wu's Big Idea

scenes.narration: Today Kinmen steel knives are sold as souvenirs, forged from the shells once fired at the island.
scenes.headline: Knives From Shells

scenes.narration: So a kitchen knife can literally be a bomb from a conflict that has never ended with a peace treaty.
scenes.headline: A Bomb In Your Kitchen

scenes.narration: That answers the hook: a beach facing China, and a knife made from China's own shells.
scenes.headline: The Hook Paid Off

scenes.narration: Today the island is also known for sorghum liquor, old village houses and visitors who come to see the war leftovers.
scenes.headline: Kinmen Today

scenes.narration: Look back at the opening picture: the skyline across the water, only a few kilometres away.
scenes.headline: Back To The Skyline

scenes.narration: The six facts: the skyline, the confused phone, the water pipe, the military rule, the speaker war, and the bomb knives.
scenes.headline: Six Facts Recap

scenes.narration: All of it comes from one simple fact of geography: Kinmen sits where Taiwan's reach meets China's coast.
scenes.headline: One Fact Of Geography

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: another place on the map that looks fake but is completely real.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow: Another Place
